title: Television Licence Fees Amendment Bill 2013
portfolio: Broadband, Communications and the Digital Economy

divisions.question: Joe Ludwig I table a statement of reasons justifying the need for these bills to be considered during these sittings and move: That these bills be now read a second time. I seek leave to have the second reading speeches and statement of reasons incorporated in _Hansard_. Leave granted. _The statement read as follows—_ STATEMENT OF REASONS FOR INTRODUCTION AND PASSAGE IN THE 2013 AUTUMN SITTINGS BROADCASTING LEGISLATION AMENDMENT (CONVERGENCE REVIEW AND OTHER MEASURES) BILL 2013 Purpose of the bills The Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Convergence Review and Other Measures) Bill 2013 amends the _Broadcasting Services Act 1992_, the _Australian Broadcasting Corporation Act 1983_ and the _Special Broadcasting Service Act 1991_ to implement initial measures arising from the government's consideration of the Convergence Review. Recognition of the current online and digital activities of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and Special Broadcasting Service, increased Australian content requirements, and a requirement for the appointment of an Indigenous non-executive director to the SBS Board. Reasons for Urgency Passage of the bill in the Autumn 2013 sittings will ensure that the communications and media policy framework continues to provide appropriate and important community safeguards in relation to the availability of quality Australian content on free-to-air television. The Convergence Review received significant interest from industry groups, businesses, academics, community groups and members of the public. The government publicly committed to implementing its initial reforms by early 2013. STATEMENT OF REASONS FOR INTRODUCTION AND PASSAGE IN THE 2013 AUTUMN SITTINGS TELEVISION LICENCE FEES AMENDMENT BILL Purpose of the bills The Television Licence Fees Amendment Bill 2013 amends the _Television Licence Fees Act 1964_ to reduce the licence fees payable by commercial television broadcasters by 50 per cent. Reasons for Urgency Passage of the bill in the Autumn

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Moved a bill cutting annual television licence fees for commercial broadcasters by 50 per cent, to a maximum of 4.5 per cent of gross earnings, as part of the government's response to the Convergence Review.

speeches.speaker: Ursula Stephens
speeches.brief: A motion was agreed to discharge and appoint senators to committees, including appointing Senators Birmingham, Cameron, Joyce, Ludlam and Thistlethwaite to the Broadcasting Legislation Joint Select Committee, and appointing Senator Ludlam as a substitute member for Senator Waters on two Environment and Communications Legislation Committee inquiries.

speeches.speaker: John Murphy
speeches.brief: Supported Australian content requirements, commercial television licence fee relief and changes to ABC and SBS charters, while arguing that media ownership concentration and the proposed international broadcasting arrangements required further consideration.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Argued that the broadcasting bills contained some supportable measures but were introduced with unreasonable haste, and proposed allowing future governments to use a tender process for the Australia Network while retaining scrutiny of the 75 per cent reach rule.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Argued that the broadcasting bills were being rushed without adequate scrutiny, supported measures on licence fees, Australian content and ABC and SBS charters, and proposed retaining contestability for Commonwealth funded international broadcasting services.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: Criticised the government's rushed media reform package, timed against a Thursday deadline, contrasting it with the extensive consultation Kim Beazley ran when introducing broadcasting law changes in 1991, noted television licence fees have already been cut 33 per cent in 2010 and 50 per cent in 2011 for a total of more than $200 million, and opposed a new provision that would let only the ABC provide Australia's international broadcasting service.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Argued that the broadcasting bills were rushed and that removing the 75 per cent reach rule could reduce media diversity and local content, particularly in regional Australia, while supporting two bills with an amendment concerning international broadcasting services.

speeches.speaker: Michael McCormack
speeches.brief: Championed local television news content in his Wagga Wagga electorate, recalled SBS television began broadcasting there on 14 July 1988, said the bill will permanently halve commercial licence fees to a maximum of 4.5 per cent of revenue worth about $140 million, and criticised a joint select committee for being given just four hours to consider evidence on the 75 per cent reach rule.

speeches.speaker: Paul Neville
speeches.brief: Recalled his own role strengthening cross-media ownership laws through the two-out-of-three rule, criticised the rushed process behind a package including a $140 million cut to television licence fees, and warned lifting the 75 per cent reach rule could hand Kerry Stokes an unfair advantage in Western Australia and require rescrambling the South Australian market.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Summed up the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill, confirming it locks in a 55 per cent Australian content quota on primary channels, permanently cuts commercial television licence fees by 50 per cent to a maximum of 4.5 per cent of gross earnings, and requires at least one Indigenous director on the SBS board.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Moved Greens amendments to double the minimum required hours of Australian content on multichannels, from 1,095 to 1,460 minutes and from 1,460 to 2,920 minutes, arguing the proposed multichannel quota of just 12 per cent is far too low given cheap overseas imports cost around 75 per cent less per hour, and cited Screen Australia research finding nine in 10 Australians value local content.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Albanese
speeches.brief: Closed the cognate debate on the two broadcasting bills, thanking members for their contributions and indicating he expected the legislation to pass with unanimous support of the House.

speeches.speaker: Joe Ludwig
speeches.brief: The speaker announced the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Convergence Review and Other Measures) Bill 2013 and the Television Licence Fees Amendment Bill 2013, which implement initial Convergence Review measures including legislating a 55% Australian content quota, capping commercial TV licences at three, and reducing broadcasters' licence fees by 50%. The coalition supported these bills but opposed excluding the Australia Network from future tender processes.
